title: Astronomers Just Created the Clearest Map of Dark Matter Using the Oldest Light in the Universe
excerpt: Astronomers used the Big Bang’s afterglow to map invisible matter with unprecedented precision.
content:
The oldest light in the universe has spent nearly 14 billion years traveling through space. Along the way, invisible matter has tugged at it, bending its path ever so slightly. Now, astronomers have turned those distortions into an extraordinary map of the invisible universe.

An international team of scientists from 30 institutions, led by the University of Chicago, analyzed observations from the South Pole Telescope (SPT) in Antarctica to produce the most sensitive map of its kind. By measuring how gravity distorted this ancient light, researchers reconstructed the distribution of ordinary and dark matter across a vast patch of the universe.

The findings, submitted to the preprint server arXiv on August 31, 2026, could help explain how the universe acquired its present-day structure, while addressing fundamental questions about dark energy, elusive particles called neutrinos, and the earliest moments of the Big Bang.

Mapping the Invisible

In its first days, the universe was enormously hot and dense. It took 380,000 years after the Big Bang for the universe to cool down enough for atoms to form and for light to travel. Photons existed before, but they only started traveling freely around that time. That ancient radiation, known as the cosmic microwave background (CMB), still permeates the universe today.

But its journey has hardly been straightforward. Massive concentrations of matter bend passing light, a phenomenon known as gravitational lensing.

Think of looking at a patterned wall through a sheet of uneven glass. By examining how the pattern appears distorted, you can work out the geometry of the glass itself (to an extent). Astronomers are doing something similar on a cosmic scale.

By measuring these tiny distortions, astronomers can determine where matter accumulated, including dark matter, whose presence is inferred by scientists through gravitational phenomena.

That’s particularly useful because dark matter accounts for roughly 85% of all matter in the universe. Most of the material astronomers want to map is invisible to conventional telescopes, and we don’t know what dark matter actually is.

×

In 2023, scientists working with the Atacama Cosmology Telescope in Chile used this technique to map dark matter across a quarter of the sky.

The new Antarctic map covers 1,500 square degrees, or roughly 3.6% of the sky. It’s not a vast swath, but it measures gravitational lensing with unprecedented sensitivity. It basically trades breadth for detail.

Researchers analyzed observations collected in 2019 and 2020 using the telescope’s 16,000-plus superconducting detectors. They measured both tiny temperature variations in the ancient radiation and its polarization—the orientation of the light’s electric field.

They also used supercomputers at Argonne National Laboratory and hundreds of simulated skies to distinguish genuine gravitational distortions from instrumental interference and radiation emitted by galaxies.

“This is the deepest map of the universe we have so far,” Yuuki Omori, the study’s lead author, said in a University of Chicago press release. “It’s like taking a photograph with very low background noise exposure.”

The Universe’s Missing Chapters

The map is particularly sensitive to matter as it existed roughly 10 billion years ago, when galaxies were growing rapidly and gravity was assembling matter into a vast cosmic web.

It’s not a photograph of the universe at a single moment in time. Rather, it captures the accumulated gravitational influence of matter that the ancient light encountered on its way to Earth.

“Scientists want to tell a coherent story that can explain everything about the universe,” Omori said. “We have a pretty good story about the beginning of the universe and a pretty good one about today, but less about the middle years.”

Combining their findings with observations from the Dark Energy Survey, the researchers measured how strongly matter clusters together in the relatively recent universe with a precision of 1.4%.

Their findings agree with predictions based on the standard model of cosmology. They also weaken some of the recent evidence suggesting that dark energy—the mysterious phenomenon driving the universe’s accelerated expansion—changes over time.

It’s not a photograph of the universe at a single moment in time. Rather, it captures the accumulated gravitational influence of matter that the ancient light encountered on its way to Earth.

The map could also help scientists weigh neutrinos, elementary particles that have no electrical charge and extremely little mass. Nuclear reactions inside stars, including our Sun, produce enormous quantities of neutrinos, while others are remnants of the Big Bang itself.

Trillions of neutrinos pass through our bodies every second without us noticing because they rarely interact with other matter. Yet despite their tiny individual masses, neutrinos are so abundant that they influence the evolution of the universe. By moving rapidly through space, they make it harder for matter to clump together, leaving a subtle but measurable imprint on the distribution of galaxies and other cosmic structures.

Their speed makes it difficult for gravity to gather them into dense structures. This suppresses the growth of cosmic structures on smaller scales, leaving a subtle but measurable imprint on the distribution of matter. In effect, astronomers can use the architecture of the universe to weigh some of its lightest particles.

Combining several astronomical datasets, the researchers estimated that the combined mass of the three known neutrino mass states is below 0.072 electron volts at a 95% confidence level, assuming the standard cosmological model. That’s less than one seven-millionth of an electron’s mass.

Echoes of the Big Bang

Perhaps the most ambitious application involves searching for primordial gravitational waves—hypothetical ripples in spacetime generated during the universe’s earliest moments.

Detecting them could provide compelling evidence for cosmic inflation, a proposed period of extraordinarily rapid expansion shortly after the universe began.

If these waves exist, they could have left distinctive swirling patterns in the polarization of the cosmic microwave background. The trouble is that gravitational lensing can produce similar patterns, potentially drowning out this much sought-after signal.

The researchers plan to use their map to remove this interference from observations made by BICEP, another experiment operating at the South Pole.

“Essentially, our map can be used to reduce the noise they see and locate the true signal,” Omori added.

The collaboration is already analyzing six years of telescope observations and working toward mapping nearly a quarter of the sky.

The same ancient light that reveals how the universe grew could ultimately help explain how it began.
